source: Fikes and Nilsson (1971) STRIPS: a new approach to the application of theorem proving to problem solving
finding: Founding formalism. An action has preconditions (must hold) and an add list and delete list (effects). A plan is a sequence of actions whose preconditions hold in turn and whose final state satisfies the goal.
numbers: Not read this session (from memory).
limits: Classical assumptions: deterministic, fully known, static.
agent_relevance: O5 work backwards: goal regression is the old form of 'start from the goal and ask what must be true first'.

source: Ghallab, Nau, Traverso (2004) Automated Planning: Theory and Practice
finding: Standard textbook. Defines classical planning as a state-transition system, forward and backward search, and PDDL-style domain and problem files.
numbers: Not read this session (from memory).
limits: Classical assumptions: deterministic, fully observed, static, known model.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary (state, action, applicable, regression) a scaffold step can borrow.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) On the Planning Abilities of Large Language Models: A Critical Investigation (PlanBench-style test)
finding: GPT-4 and earlier GPT models plan poorly on IPC-style domains even in simple Blocksworld, and chain of thought barely helped.
numbers: Blocksworld, 600 instances. GPT-4 plan generation: one-shot natural language 206/600 (34.3%), zero-shot 210/600 (34.6%), one-shot COT 214/600 (35.6%); PDDL prompts 75/600 (12.5%) and 106/600 (17.6%). GPT-3.5 37/600 (6.1%) zero-shot. Average over all domains about 12% for GPT-4.
limits: Only GPT family and one BLOOM test (4/250). Instances are unobfuscated, so memory may help.
agent_relevance: A plain model is a weak forward simulator of preconditions and effects; the scaffold must supply state tracking.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) On the Planning Abilities of Large Language Models: A Critical Investigation: obfuscation and Logistics
finding: Renaming actions and objects (Mystery Blocksworld) destroys performance, which points to pattern matching more than rule application.
numbers: GPT-4 Mystery Blocksworld one-shot natural language 26/600 (4.3%), zero-shot 1/600 (0.16%). Logistics (200 instances) one-shot 28/200 (14%), zero-shot 15/200 (7.5%).
limits: Obfuscation uses a fixed mapping; later work added random strings (see c07).
agent_relevance: Test the agent on renamed or abstract versions of a task. If it falls, it is recalling, not simulating effects.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) On the Planning Abilities of Large Language Models: A Critical Investigation: human baseline
finding: Humans do the easy Blocksworld task far better than GPT-4.
numbers: 50 participants, one random Blocksworld instance each: 39 (78%) gave a valid plan; 35 of those 39 (89.7%) gave an optimal plan. 11 failed.
limits: One instance per person, primed with one example, crowd-sourced; not matched to the LLM prompt.
agent_relevance: The gap between easy-for-humans and hard-for-LLMs is the clearest argument for an external state tracker.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) On the Planning Abilities of Large Language Models: A Critical Investigation: fine-tuning and verifier backprompting
finding: Fine-tuning gave a small gain; a sound verifier in a loop gave a large one.
numbers: Fine-tuned GPT-3 on 1,000 Blocksworld instances solved 122/600 (about 20%). GPT-4 with VAL backprompting (up to 15 rounds): 82% Blocksworld, 70% Logistics (179 instances); average rounds 3.68 and 3.31. Mystery Blocksworld stayed poor.
limits: Logistics subset limited to instances solvable in under 550 search steps. Needs a PDDL model of the domain to run VAL.
agent_relevance: A symbolic checker of preconditions in the loop is worth more than extra training.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? A Preliminary Evaluation of OpenAI's o1 on PlanBench
finding: A reasoning model (o1) jumps far above LLMs on Blocksworld but is not robust.
numbers: 600 instances: o1-preview 97.8% Blocksworld, 52.8% Mystery BW, 37.3% Randomized Mystery BW (random-string names). Logistics 94% and 52% obfuscated. Best earlier LLM, LLaMA 3.1 405B, 62.6% Blocksworld. Plans of 20+ steps (110 instances): 23.63%. Fast Downward 100% in seconds.
limits: Early o1 access, small token budget; accuracy still falls with plan length and obfuscation.
agent_relevance: Longer reasoning helps action-effect tracking but still decays with horizon; keep subgoal decomposition.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) o1 on unsolvable instances
finding: o1 rarely says a problem is impossible, and sometimes calls solvable ones impossible.
numbers: 100 unsolvable instances. Blocksworld: 27% correctly flagged, 19% returned an empty plan, 54% returned an impossible full plan. Randomized Mystery BW: 16% flagged, 5% empty plan, 79% full impossible plan; 11.5% of solvable instances wrongly called impossible.
limits: One model, 100 unsolvable items.
agent_relevance: The agent needs an explicit 'goal unreachable' check from backward search; the model rarely gives it.

source: Valmeekam, Stechly, Gundawar, Kambhampati (2024) Planning in Strawberry Fields
finding: o1 beats LLMs but at high cost; putting o1 in a loop with a sound verifier (LRM-Modulo) adds correctness guarantees and more accuracy.
numbers: LRM-Modulo, up to 10 iterations: o1-preview hard Blocksworld 98.2% (saturates in 7 rounds), graph colouring 94%, Sokoban 12.7% to 43.6%. TravelPlanner sole-planning (180 items): o1-preview 10%, o1-mini 1.67%, prior best 4.4%. Calendar scheduling: o1-mini 94% for $2.70; GPT-4o-mini with 50 modulo rounds 97% for $2.48.
limits: Cost limited rounds to 10; domains with formal checkers only.
agent_relevance: A cheap model plus a sound checker can beat a costly reasoner: supports a verifier loop over longer thinking.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: Position paper: LLMs are approximate retrievers, good as idea generators, not sound planners. Pair them with external critics. Self-critique is of questionable value.
numbers: Cites 82% Blocksworld and 70% Logistics with VAL backprompting in 15 rounds; about 10% on Mystery BW; TravelPlanner best prompting 0.7% (GPT-3.5-turbo).
limits: Position paper; results are the group's own earlier ones.
agent_relevance: The main design statement behind a generate-then-verify scaffold.

source: Liu et al. (2023) LLM+P: Empowering LLMs with Optimal Planning Proficiency
finding: The LLM only translates the task into a PDDL problem file (with one worked example); Fast Downward solves it; the plan is translated back. Far better than asking the LLM to plan.
numbers: 7 IPC robot domains, 20 tasks each, GPT-4. Blocksworld: LLM+P 90% vs LLM-as-planner 20%. Tree of Thoughts timed out in most cases. Without the example problem and PDDL, LLM+P failed to produce correct problem files.
limits: Needs a human-written domain PDDL; failures were mis-specified problem files (missing initial conditions). Table garbled in extraction, so only the Blocksworld pair is quoted.
agent_relevance: Use the LLM for formalisation, a tool for search. Needs a worked example in context.

source: Guan et al. (2023) Leveraging Pre-trained LLMs to Construct and Utilize World Models for Model-based Task Planning (LLM-DM)
finding: GPT-4 writes the PDDL action model (preconditions, effects) with human correction; a classical planner then plans far better than the LLM alone.
numbers: Household and Logistics. LLM planner only: 15% Household, 0% Logistics. LLM backprompted by VAL with the LLM-built model: 48% and 33%. Fast Downward with the LLM-built model: 95% (failures only from goal translation) and 100%. Up to 8 feedback rounds; GPT-4 often repeated the same plan after feedback.
limits: 27 Household and 21 Logistics tasks; human experts corrected the domain model; object types fixed. Table cell assignment read from garbled text.
agent_relevance: Action models can be elicited from a model then checked by a human once; strong case for O5 with an explicit model.

source: Silver et al. (2024) Generalized Planning in PDDL Domains with Pretrained LLMs
finding: GPT-4 writes a Python generalized plan from a PDDL domain and a few training tasks, debugged with VAL feedback; solves much larger tasks than prompted planning.
numbers: Fraction of 30 evaluation tasks solved (10 seeds): GPT-4 Delivery 0.90, Forest 1.00, Gripper 0.90, Ferry 0.80, Spanner 0.10, Miconic 0.01, Heavy 0.60. No chain of thought: Delivery 0.70. No debug: Delivery 0.10, Forest 0.62. Names obfuscated: about 0.10 to 0.11. GPT-3.5 near 0 except Forest 0.32. Error types in training: Python exception 40%, plan semantics 34%, syntax 13%, timeout 13%.
limits: Domains are simple; Miconic fails; evaluation tasks are far larger than training tasks.
agent_relevance: Programs as plans: the model writes a rule, a checker runs it. Names matter again, so pattern use.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning
finding: Chain-of-thought gains in Blocksworld exist only when the prompt is tailored to the exact problem class; they do not generalise.
numbers: Accuracy GPT-4-Turbo / Claude-3-Opus / GPT-4: zero-shot 19.1 / 9.96 / 3.83; zero-shot CoT 21 / 10.34 / 4.98; universal algorithm prompt 37.1 / 37.1 / 51.3; table-to-stack stacking prompt 40.6 / 24.5 / 59.3 (261 instances for GPT-4). Self-consistency lowered performance. Planner 100%.
limits: Blocksworld mainly, plus synthetic tasks. Gains vanish when the goal moves outside the exemplar class.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a generic step-by-step prompt. A planning step needs the exact procedure for the problem class.

source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) Can LLMs Really Improve by Self-critiquing Their Own Plans?
finding: GPT-4 as its own plan verifier gives many false positives and does worse than a sound verifier.
numbers: 100 Blocksworld instances. LLM+LLM backprompting 55%; LLM+VAL backprompting 88%; no backprompting 40%. LLM verifier correct on 61/100; 38 false positives (84.45% of invalid plans passed as valid); 54 true positives; 7 false negatives. Feedback granularity (binary vs detailed VAL) changed results little (50-instance runs between 74% and 86%).
limits: One model, temperature 0, one domain.
agent_relevance: Self-critique on precondition checks is unreliable; use programmatic checks when possible.

source: Xie et al. (2024) TravelPlanner: A Benchmark for Real-World Planning with Language Agents
finding: Multi-constraint planning with tools was almost out of reach for agents; the best was under 1 percent.
numbers: 1,225 queries (45 train, 180 validation, 1,000 test). GPT-4-Turbo final pass rate 0.6%. 20 graduate students annotated the reference plans.
limits: Micro and macro constraint rates exist but were not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Failure is tracking many constraints at once, an argument for an explicit constraint ledger.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) NATURAL PLAN: Benchmarking LLMs on Natural Language Planning
finding: Natural-language planning with full information is hard and drops with size; self-correction hurts; many examples help only long-context models.
numbers: 5-shot: Trip Planning GPT-4 31.1%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 34.8%, GPT-3.5 7.3%, GPT-4o 3.7%; Meeting Planning GPT-4 47%, GPT-4o 45.2%, Gemini 39.1%; Calendar Gemini 48.9%. All models below 5% at 10 cities. Gemini 1.5 Pro trip planning 2.7% at 1 shot to 39.9% at 800 shots; GPT-4 peaked at 20 shots. Self-correction lowered accuracy for all models, more for the stronger ones.
limits: Exact-match scoring; mid-2024 models.
agent_relevance: Self-correction without a checker lowers accuracy. Problem size matters more than domain.

source: Gundawar et al. (2024) Robust Planning with Compound LLM Architectures: An LLM-Modulo Approach
finding: Wrapping an LLM in a loop with sound critics raises accuracy on scheduling and travel planning, and every returned plan passes the critics.
numbers: TravelPlanner: GPT-4o 8.33% to 23.89%, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 4.4% to 25%. Trip Planning: GPT-4o 3.43% to 40%; GPT-4o-mini 6.18% to 12.06%; Claude 39.43% to 47%. Meeting: GPT-4o 49.1% to 59.8%, Claude 57.1% to 69.5%, mini 32.8% to 51.9%. Calendar: mini 36.9% to 61.6%. GPT-4o-mini on TravelPlanner: CoT 2.2%, ReAct 0%, LLM-Modulo 15% (10 rounds).
limits: Critics hand-written per domain; 10 rounds; temperature 0.
agent_relevance: The plan-verify-reprompt loop is the main driver; critics are encoded constraint checks.

source: Kokel, Katz, Srinivas, Sohrabi (2025) ACPBench: Reasoning about Action, Change, and Planning
finding: Tests the atomic skills inside planning (applicability, progression, reachability, validation, justification, landmarks). Models are weak on the hardest ones.
numbers: 7 tasks, 13 domains, 22 LLMs plus o1. GPT-4o with COT 2-shot: 78.40% on multiple choice, lowest 52.50% on validation. o1-preview: 87.31% MCQ, lowest 63.08%; no notable gain on boolean questions (chance 50%). Fine-tuned Granite-code 8B: boolean 51.43% to 95.71%, MCQ 19.18% to 94.29%, carried to 5 unseen domains.
limits: Tasks generated from PDDL; fine-tuning data from the same generator.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that the 'is this action applicable now' check is where models slip; use an explicit check step.

source: Oswald et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Planning Domain Generators
finding: Models can write PDDL domains from text, but few equal the reference.
numbers: 7 LLMs, 9 domains, 3 description types. Best (LLaMA-2-70b) valid PDDL in 94% of domains and 25% heuristically equivalent to the reference. Chat (RLHF) LLaMA models did worse than base. Extra predicate hints helped StarCoder by about 10%, not LLaMA.
limits: Old open models; scored by comparing plan sets.
agent_relevance: Domain modelling is the bottleneck; have a human check an action model once before relying on it.

source: Huang et al. (2022) Language Models as Zero-Shot Planners
finding: Plans from large LMs look sensible but often break action rules; mapping each step to the nearest admissible action raises executability but lowers human-judged correctness.
numbers: VirtualHome, 88 held-out tasks, 7 scenes. Executability 18% to 79% after translation to admissible actions, with some drop in correctness.
limits: Human correctness ratings, small task set.
agent_relevance: Executability and correctness differ; the agent should check both applicability and goal fit.

source: Goebel and Zips (2025) Can LLM-Reasoning Models Replace Classical Planning? A Benchmark Study
finding: Models prompted directly with PDDL files do fine on simple tasks but fail on resources, state tracking and constraints; reasoning variants help moderately.
numbers: Success over five domains: GPT-o1 63.4%, Claude Sonnet 3.7 Thinking 63.4%, Claude 3.7 58.1%, Gemini 2 Flash Thinking 35.5% vs Flash 23.7%, Claude Sonnet 3.5 41.94%. Execution fidelity: GPT-o1 73.4%, Llama 405B 13.9%. Fast Downward 100%.
limits: Small benchmark; early-2025 models; planning time up to 160 s.
agent_relevance: Thinking models help but plans may still contain unexecutable steps; add execution fidelity checks.

source: Teaching LLMs to Plan: Logical Chain-of-Thought Instruction Tuning for Symbolic Planning (PDDL-Instruct, 2025)
finding: Training models to reason explicitly about precondition satisfaction and effect application, with VAL feedback, raises plan validity a lot.
numbers: Llama-3-8B baseline Blocksworld 28%, Mystery BW 1%, Logistics 11%. With PDDL-Instruct (detailed feedback, 15 iterations): 94%, 64%, 79%. Detailed feedback beat binary by 5, 15 and 7 points on those domains.
limits: Needs training, so not a pure scaffold; same-domain test.
agent_relevance: Explicit precondition-and-effect steps in text drove the gain; a prompt-only version can copy the format.

source: Dagan, Keller, Lascarides (2023) Dynamic Planning with an LLM
finding: LLM-DP: the LLM turns the task into PDDL and a planner plans, in a loop for ALFWorld.
numbers: Not opened; numbers not recorded.
limits: From memory.
agent_relevance: Another instance of LLM-as-formaliser plus a classical planner.

source: Ahn et al. (2022) Do As I Can, Not As I Say (SayCan)
finding: Combine LM step proposals with learned affordance values that say whether the action is feasible now.
numbers: Not opened; numbers not recorded.
limits: From memory.
agent_relevance: The affordance value plays the role of a precondition check on each candidate step.

source: Pallagani et al. (2024) On the Prospects of Incorporating LLMs in Automated Planning and Scheduling
finding: Survey that sorts LLM roles in planning: translation, plan generation, model construction, interactive planning, heuristics.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: From memory.
agent_relevance: A taxonomy to check the agent's use of a planner against.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2022) PlanBench: An Extensible Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Planning and Reasoning about Change
finding: Introduces the PlanBench task suite: plan generation, optimal planning, verification, reuse, generalisation, replanning, plan-execution reasoning, goal shuffling.
numbers: GPT-4 Blocksworld, 600 instances: plan generation 206 (34.3%), cost-optimal 198 (33%), plan verification 191 (31.8%). Instruct-GPT3: 41 (6.8%), 35 (5.8%), 4 (0.6%).
limits: Mapping of the remaining task rows was garbled in extraction and not quoted.
agent_relevance: Verification at about 32% matches generation, hinting early that self-checking is not reliable.
